name: Victor Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, and nothing gets linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a full-stack developer at a climate-data startup, about forty people. We make software that reads energy meters in office buildings and tells the owners where they're wasting heat. On a normal day I'm building dashboards in the morning, fixing data pipelines after lunch, and arguing about charts with our designer, Ana, at four. I like that the work has a point beyond making someone rich.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do AI tools figure in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, all day. I have an assistant open in my editor and another one I've set up to write the first draft of our data checks. I probably write half the code I did two years ago and review twice as much. Some days it feels like being a site foreman for very fast, slightly drunk builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, because I've bet a lot of my own time on these tools. At work I'd say they still save us real hours on the boring stuff, so keep using them. Online I'd probably admit the hype was overblown and that I was part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, nothing bad happens to me. I'd still be a decent developer who's faster than most with the tools, at a startup that's doing fine, in a city with lots of tech jobs. My partner and I would carry on as we are, with plenty saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep using the assistants where they help. I'd probably drop the fancier experiments and spend that time learning more about building physics, which is where our product's real value is. Money stays the same: save, invest a bit, take one good holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, slightly deflated. It's like training for a marathon that gets cancelled; you're fit, but you wanted to run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were part of the hype. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I gave a talk at a local meetup last year called something like 'Your team will be half the size'. If AI stalls, I'd owe a few people a drink and an apology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there any pressures in your life that don't depend on AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Startup funding, mainly. We have about eighteen months of money in the bank, and if the next round doesn't come, I'd be job-hunting anyway. But with my savings and the number of firms nearby, that wouldn't scare me much.

say: I'd admit the hype was **overblown**, and that I was part of it.
I'd say the tools still **save real hours** on boring work, so keep using them.
think: Nothing bad happens to me: **decent job**, plenty saved, lots of firms nearby.
The only real risk is the startup's **eighteen months** of funding.
do: Keep using the **assistants** where they actually help.
Spend spare time learning **building physics** instead of AI experiments.
Keep saving and investing at the **same rate**.
feel: **Calm** and slightly deflated, like a cancelled marathon.
S0.quote: I gave a talk at a local meetup last year called something like 'Your team will be half the size'. If AI stalls, I'd owe a few people a drink.
fieldNote: He has **bet his time** on AI tools and would feel let down rather than relieved.
His only real pressure is **startup funding**, which savings and local jobs cover.
He would redirect his curiosity toward **building physics**.

steps.text: Keep building energy dashboards with the coding assistants
Study building physics instead of chasing new AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when we need rules: the gains from AI should go to workers as shorter weeks and to the public as tax, not just to shareholders. At work I'd be the person helping everyone else get good with the tools. Online I'd share how-to guides and also argue for a four-day week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one is good for me. I'm already the person on my team who uses these tools best, so I'd probably get more responsibility, not less. The bit that bothers me is that I know which colleagues won't keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up AI agents for our data checks and test writing in the first three months, and I'd run lunchtime sessions so the whole team learns. I'd ask for a raise or a lead title in the first year, because I'd be doing more. And I'd join the campaign for a four-day week, because if the work shrinks, the hours should too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a small guilty knot. I'd be doing well out of something that's hurting people I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the colleagues you think won't keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana, our designer, for one. She's brilliant, but she hates the tools and says they flatten everything into the same beige. I'd want her kept, and I'd be loud about it, but the founders might not listen to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favour regulation, but you'd also be automating your own team's work. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they fit, but I see why it looks odd. If I don't automate it, a competitor will, and then the whole company goes. What I want is for the savings to be shared, so I'd do the automating and the arguing at the same time.

say: I'd say AI gains should go to **workers and the public**, not just shareholders.
I'd share guides online and argue for a **four-day week**.
think: This one is **good for me**, as the team's best tool user.
I already know **which colleagues** won't keep up.
do: Set up **AI agents** for data checks and test writing within three months.
Run **lunchtime sessions** so the whole team learns the tools.
Ask for a **raise or lead title** and back the four-day week campaign.
feel: **Excited**, with a small guilty knot about colleagues who would be hurt.
S1.quote: If I don't automate our data checks, a competitor will, and then the whole company goes.
fieldNote: He openly holds **automating and arguing** for shared gains at the same time.
His **guilt** centres on a designer colleague who rejects the tools.
His job looks **safer here**, so his mood rests on his own gain.

steps.text: Set up AI agents for data checks and test writing
Run lunchtime sessions teaching colleagues the coding tools
Join the campaign for a four-day working week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest economic shock of our lives and we should treat it like a war or a pandemic: public money, fast. At work I'd say let's be honest about what happens to our jobs. Online I'd push for a windfall tax on the AI companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my developer job goes. If AI can do any thinking work as well as me and cheaper, then being 'good with the tools' lasts maybe a year. I'm twenty-seven with savings and no kids, so I'm one of the luckiest people this could happen to, but I'd still be out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd save harder and shift toward the hands-on side of our product: installing the meters and sensors in buildings, which gets about three more years before robots. I'd do a short course in electrical installation in 2027. After it arrives, I'd work as an installer and push hard for public income support for everyone, not just people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but oddly focused. I'd feel like I had to move fast and not look down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the sensors in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know what they do and why they matter, so I'm not starting from zero. Climbing into a ceiling at a hospital to fit a meter is something no AI does in 2028, and I'd be useful to people I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam teaches music at a secondary school, so honestly Sam would laugh and say welcome to an unpredictable career. We'd be fine on Sam's pay plus my savings for a while, which makes me braver than I'd otherwise be.

say: I'd say treat this like a **pandemic-scale shock**, with public money, fast.
I'd push online for a **windfall tax** on AI companies.
think: Being good with the tools lasts **maybe a year** once AGI can code.
I'm one of the **luckiest** people this could hit, but still out of work.
do: **Save harder** before 2028 and do an electrical course in 2027.
Move to **installing meters** and sensors, which get about three more years.
Campaign for **public income support** for everyone after it lands.
feel: **Nervous** but focused, moving fast and not looking down.
S2.quote: Climbing into a ceiling at a hospital to fit a meter is something no AI does in 2028.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the coding job** but feels in control of a plan.
He uses the **three-year robot gap** by moving to hands-on installation he already knows.
His partner's **teaching pay** makes him braver about the jump.

steps.text: Take a short electrical installation course in 2027
Move to fitting energy meters and sensors in buildings
Campaign for public income support funded by AI firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and no excuse. I'd want the government to start funding retraining now, and I'd say so at every meetup I go to. At work, I'd say we should plan which parts of the company survive and how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my coding job still goes, around 2031, but I'd have five years to earn well and set up the next thing. I'd be thirty-two. I think I'd end up running installation crews or doing energy audits on site, with AI doing the analysis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep coding and push hard on the AI side of the job, because it pays well right now. In year two I'd start doing energy audits on weekends, paid, to learn the site side. I'd put a chunk of savings into a small share of a local heat-pump installer that a friend runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It's like having a deadline at work: it focuses you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a lot of plans. Is anything you'd lose sleep over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents, actually. My dad's an accountant at a small firm, and he's fifty-five. Five years is no time for him, and I'd probably end up helping them financially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that do to your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It splits them. I'd want to keep a year for myself and the rest would go between the installer business and a fund for my parents if they need it.

say: I'd say five years means **no excuse** not to fund retraining now.
I'd want the company to plan **which parts survive** and how.
think: My coding job still **goes around 2031**, after five good-earning years.
I'd likely run **installation crews** or on-site energy audits by then.
do: Keep coding and lean into the **AI side** while it pays well.
Do paid **weekend energy audits** from year two.
Put savings into a friend's **heat-pump installer** business.
feel: **Anxious** in a workable way, like a deadline that sharpens focus.
S3.quote: My dad's an accountant at a small firm, and he's fifty-five. Five years is no time for my dad.
fieldNote: His worry shifts from himself to his **father's accounting job**.
He would **split savings** between his own cushion, a business stake and his parents.
He plans a hands-on **second career** before his coding income ends.

steps.text: Do paid weekend energy audits from the second year
Buy a small stake in a friend's heat-pump installer
Set aside a fund to support his parents if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade to design a fair transition, and that it would be shameful to waste it. I'd push for public training programmes and stronger unions in tech. At work I'd say let's enjoy the good years but not pretend they're forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years is a lot for me. I'd be thirty-seven, with a solid decade of good pay behind me and time to build something hands-on. I'm not sure I'd even need to leave tech early; I'd just move steadily toward the physical side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, honestly, I'd keep going much as now, using the tools hard and saving well. I'd put money into index funds and the heat-pump installer. Around year four I'd start the move into on-site energy work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more for others than myself. I'd mostly worry about people who don't have my options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd actually move, with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope so. I'm the type who gets bored, so I think I'd want to move before I had to, maybe around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year version you'd find harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The waiting. With a long runway, people argue for years about whether it's real. I'd find it hard watching friends refuse to plan.

say: I'd say a decade is time to design a **fair transition**, and wasting it is shameful.
I'd push for **public training** and stronger unions in tech.
think: Ten years gives me a **solid decade** of good pay and time to build.
I might not leave tech early, just **move steadily** to the physical side.
do: Keep using the tools hard and **saving well** in the first year.
Invest in **index funds** and the heat-pump installer.
Start the move into **on-site energy work** around year four.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for others without his options than for himself.
S4.quote: With a long runway, people argue for years about whether AGI is real, and I'd find it hard watching friends refuse to plan.
fieldNote: His own job looks **safe for years**, so his unease is mostly for others.
He expects boredom to push him to **move before he has to**.
He sees **denial among friends** as the hardest part of a long warning.

steps.text: Keep coding with AI tools and saving well
Invest in index funds and the heat-pump installer
Move into on-site energy auditing around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my parents and a lot of my friends have no time to move. For me, what would help is a short, paid electrical course and a decent public income floor while I switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we owe each other. People like me will do fine in most of these pictures, and I think that comes with a duty to fight for the ones who won't.

headlineQuote: Some days it feels like being a site foreman for very fast, slightly drunk builders.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old** full-stack developer at a climate-data startup who uses AI tools all day.
He is **progressive** and wants AI gains shared through tax, unions and shorter weeks.
He sees Steady Disruption as **good for him**, but feels guilty about colleagues left behind.
In the AGI pictures he plans to move into **hands-on energy work** like fitting meters.
His worries turn toward his **father** and friends with fewer options than him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mainly because his parents and many friends would have no time to move.
whatWouldHelp: A **short paid electrical course** and a decent public income floor while switching.
